newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's post-war politics dominated by LDP.
newsitem.headline: Japan's post-war politics dominated by LDP.

text.p: The history of Japanese politics since World War Two can be boiled down to a battle for control of just one party, the still-dominant Liberal Democrats.

The October 20 general election is again an affair centering on the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), since it is in effect a three-way race between Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's LDP and two groups led by LDP defectors -- Ichiro Ozawa's Shinshinto and Yukio Hatoyama's new Democratic Party.
The same battle was first waged in the decade after the war when Shigeru Yoshida, a pre-war career diplomat, was the top man in Japanese politics.
Except for two Socialist-led coalitions in 1947-48, the cigar-smoking Yoshida and his conservative Liberal Party held power until 1954.
During that time he presided over the 1950 founding of Japan's present-day military, the 1952 San Francisco Peace Treaty and the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.
The Socialist Party, meanwhile, vacillated between taking part in government and opposing military ties with the United States.
In 1951 it split into rival right and left wings only to merge again into the Japan Socialist Party in 1955.
That triggered the merger of the two big conservative parties to found the Liberal Democratic Party in the same year.

In 1956 Hayato Ikeda took office, telling Japan to forget about political ideology and concentrate on "double income" prosperity, a formula that wildly succeeded in turning Japan into a world economic powerhouse.
With living standards rising and the electorate content, Japan entered a period of political stability that lasted through the early 1970s.
The party perfected a triangular system to perpetuate LDP rule -- voter support from farm areas, financial support from big firms and administrative support from the bureaucracy.

In 1972, the party began 20 years of infighting but managed to stay in power the entire time. The legendary Kakuei Tanaka was among those in the prime minister's seat but even out of office enjoyed huge power in the country and the party.
Until 1982, no LDP prime minister had more than two years in office, which saw Japan through two oil crises and a 1976 payoff scandal involving the U.S. aircraft firm Lockheed.
In 1982, the revolving door stopped with Yashuhiro Nakasone managing to stay in power for five years, delivering the biggest LDP election victory in decades.
Nakasone duly handed over power to Noboru Takeshita in 1987, but trouble loomed.
In less than two years Takeshita was among those felled by a scandal in which politicians accepted shares from a employment firm in exchange for some insider help.
In desperation, the premiership first went to Sosuke Uno, who was immediately brought down in a messy geisha affair.
The LDP's Tanaka faction then turned to "Mr. Clean", Toshiki Kaifu, who led it to victory in a 1990 election.

But the victory did not save him from being deposed by Tanaka powerbrokers who gave the premiership to Kiichi Miyazawa. But his economic expertise failed to stop the bursting of Japan's economic bubble.

By early 1993, the LDP was rife with dissent. Mass defections from the party deprived it of its majority in parliament for the first time since its founding 38 years earlier, and Miyazawa was toppled in a no-confidence motion.
The LDP lost badly in the July 1993 elections and an anti-LDP coalition came to power.
But when the Socialists walked away from that coalition in 1994, the LDP came back to power and appears set to remain the dominant force in Japanese politics.
